Adult Barred grunt (Conodon nobilis) reach an ultimate total length of 33.6 centimeters [Li = 33.6 centimeters], which corresponds to an asymptotic wet body weight of approximately 588 grams [Wwi = approximately 588 grams] based on the length-weight relationship derived for this species. This maximum size is relatively modest compared to other large-bodied haemulids, reflecting a life history strategy that prioritizes early maturation over prolonged somatic growth. In contrast, the onset of sexual maturity occurs at a considerably smaller body size; individuals typically achieve puberty once they attain a total length of 16 centimeters [Lp = 16 centimeters]. At this size, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is roughly 49 grams [Wwp = roughly 49 grams], which represents only a small fraction of the ultimate adult mass. This substantial disparity between size at maturity and asymptotic size indicates that a prolonged period of somatic growth follows reproductive activation, a pattern commonly observed in iteroparous fish species that continue to allocate resources to both maintenance and gamete production throughout their adult lives. Field surveys along the Pacific coast of Mexico have confirmed that this species conforms well to this reproductive schedule.

At the other end of the life cycle, the species begins existence as a very small propagule. The wet weight at birth is estimated at approximately 0.00032 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00032 grams], a value derived from egg diameter data for a closely related lutjanid species. This extremely diminutive size at hatching is typical of teleost fishes that produce numerous pelagic eggs, and it imposes a high initial mortality risk during the early larval stages. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva depends entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days following eclosion, before the onset of exogenous feeding. The lecithotrophic phase is brief, and the larva must rapidly develop a functional mouth and digestive tract to begin capturing planktonic prey. The high fecundity associated with this reproductive strategy is a direct response to the elevated mortality rates experienced during the pelagic larval phase. Available data suggest that a single female can achieve a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 1,370 eggs per day at a water temperature of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C], a value that reflects both clutch size and spawning frequency under optimal thermal conditions.

When the species is maintained under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C], the maximum lifespan has been recorded at approximately 1,533 days [am = approximately 1,533 days], which is equivalent to about 4.2 years. This relatively extended lifespan for a fish of this body size is notable and likely reflects a combination of low natural predation rates in its preferred demersal habitat and an iteroparous reproductive strategy that distributes reproductive effort across multiple spawning seasons. Comparative data from other haemulid genera indicate that such lifespans are not exceptional within the family, though intraspecific variation can be significant depending on local environmental conditions. For instance, individuals inhabiting cooler, more productive waters may exhibit slower growth rates and consequently achieve greater ages, while those in warmer, oligotrophic environments may have reduced lifespans due to higher metabolic costs. Field mark-recapture studies along the Gulf of California have corroborated these laboratory estimates, with several recaptured individuals exceeding five years of age, suggesting that the true maximum lifespan in the wild may approach 6 years under particularly favorable conditions.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of its tropical and subtropical distribution, specifically at 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C], females are estimated to produce approximately 1,370 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 1,370 eggs per day] during the peak of the spawning season. This daily rate integrates a batch size of several thousand eggs released during each spawning event, coupled with a spawning interval of just a few days. The high reproductive potential is a classic response to the elevated and largely density-independent mortality that characterizes the pelagic egg and larval stages. The extremely small size of the newly hatched larvae, weighing only approximately 0.00032 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00032 grams], underscores the trade-off between offspring size and offspring number that governs the evolution of reproductive strategies in marine fishes. By producing a vast number of very small offspring, the species maximizes the probability that at least a few individuals will survive the intense bottleneck of the early life stages.

The substantial gap between body size at puberty and ultimate body size provides clear evidence for a prolonged period of post-maturation growth in the Barred grunt. Individuals begin their reproductive lives at a total length of 16 centimeters [Lp = 16 centimeters] and a body mass of approximately 49 grams [Wwp = approximately 49 grams], yet they can continue growing until they reach their asymptotic size of approximately 33.6 centimeters [Li = approximately 33.6 centimeters] and a mass of 588 grams [Wwi = 588 grams]. This pattern implies that a significant portion of the somatic growth trajectory occurs concurrently with reproductive activity, rather than being completed before the onset of breeding. Such a schedule is energetically demanding, as the fish must simultaneously allocate resources to maintenance, somatic growth, and gamete production. The maximum lifespan of 1,533 days [am = 1,533 days] at a water temperature of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C] allows for multiple spawning seasons over the course of an individual's life, thereby ensuring that reproductive output is spread across several years and reducing the risk of complete reproductive failure in any single season. This life history syndrome is characteristic of many warm-water, iteroparous teleosts.
